title: Samson Raphael Hirsch
hookLine: Torah joined with worldly life, a founder of modern Orthodoxy

lines: THE TORAH AND A GEOMETRY BOOK.
cards: A schoolboy's bag in Frankfurt. Inside it, a book of the Torah in Hebrew. Next to it, a German grammar, a geometry book, a history of the ancient world.
He'll study all of them today, in one building, from teachers who keep the Sabbath and the dietary laws without bending them.

Nobody there thinks the geometry is a threat to the Torah, or the Torah an excuse to skip the geometry. The rabbi who built this school believed both belonged in one bag. His name was Samson Raphael Hirsch.

teach.h: THE TORAH IS THE MEASURE OF THE TIMES.
teach.b: Hirsch faced the same crisis as yesterday's reformers: young German Jews drifting from Judaism as they entered German life. But he drew the opposite conclusion about the law.
The Torah, he said, was not something to adjust to the times; it was the measure by which the times are judged.
So he would not change the service or loosen the commandments. Yet he was no stranger to the modern world.
He wrote fine German prose, admired German poets, and wanted Jewish children to learn science, languages and history alongside Torah. His motto came from the Mishnah.

teach.h: TORAH WITH THE WAY OF THE LAND.
teach.b: In Pirkei Avot, Rabban Gamliel, the son of Rabbi Judah the Prince, says Torah study is beautiful together with derekh eretz, the way of the land, meaning a worldly occupation, because the effort of both keeps a person from sin.
Hirsch took those words, Torah im derekh eretz, and made them a whole program.
For him, derekh eretz meant more than a job: the whole of a cultured, working, civic life, lived inside the commandments rather than beside them.
A Jew could be a doctor, a merchant, a reader of poetry and a citizen, and keep every law of the Sabbath while doing it.
He built schools in Frankfurt to teach exactly that, and wrote a long commentary on the Torah that is still read. People often name him as a founder of what came to be called modern Orthodoxy.
Not every traditional rabbi shared his openness to secular learning, and Orthodox Jews still discuss how far his program reaches.
But his answer was clear: keep the Torah whole, and bring the world inside it.

how: Modern Orthodox Jewish schools today commonly teach a dual curriculum of Torah and general studies, and some trace that model to Hirsch's motto, Torah im derekh eretz.

practice: Think of the ordinary work in front of you today and one teaching you hold dear, from the Torah or wherever you draw wisdom: honesty, rest, kindness to the stranger.
Ask where in that work the teaching could live, not beside it but inside it.
